statement: For an [(∞,1)-operad](c:infinity-1-operad) $P$, the operadic Grothendieck construction is an equivalence from [algebras](c:infinity-algebra-over-an-infinity-1-operad) over $P$ in $(\infty,1)$-categories to [coCartesian fibrations](c:cocartesian-fibration-of-infinity-1-operads) over $P$.

hypotheses.text: $P$ is an [(∞,1)-operad](c:infinity-1-operad).

conclusion: Sending a $P$-algebra to its total operadic fibration over $P$ is an equivalence of $(\infty,1)$-categories.

proofs.name: Dendroidal straightening
proofs.slogan: Model $P$ by a dendroidal $\infty$-operad, build the Grothendieck construction from algebras to coCartesian fibrations, and show that it is an equivalence.
proofs.scope: Outline of the published proof, for $P$ modeled as a dendroidal $\infty$-operad. The model-categorical verifications rest on the cited work.

roles.why: The operad $P$ is the base over which algebras and fibrations are compared.

steps.slogan: Model the operad $P$ by a dendroidal $\infty$-operad $X$.
steps.detail: Choose a dendroidal set $X$ that models $P$, and let $\mathrm{hc}\tau_d(X)$ be the simplicial operad that it presents. Algebras over $P$ in $(\infty,1)$-categories are algebras over $\mathrm{hc}\tau_d(X)$ in $\infty$-categories.

steps.slogan: Define coCartesian fibrations of dendroidal sets over $X$.
steps.detail: The definition extends Lurie's [coCartesian fibrations](c:cocartesian-fibration-of-infinity-1-operads) of simplicial sets. It asks for coCartesian lifts of the operations of $X$, for every choice of lifts of their inputs. These fibrations form an $(\infty,1)$-category $\mathrm{coCart}(X)$.

steps.slogan: Turn an algebra into a coCartesian fibration by the Grothendieck construction.
steps.detail: The generalized [Grothendieck construction](c:grothendieck-construction) of the cited paper sends an algebra $A$ to a dendroidal set over $X$ whose fiber over a color $c$ is the $\infty$-category $A(c)$. The structure maps of $A$ give the coCartesian lifts. Over a unary operad this is the $(\infty,1)$-Grothendieck construction.

steps.slogan: Show that this construction is an equivalence onto coCartesian fibrations over $X$.
steps.detail: The cited paper proves that the construction and a straightening functor give an equivalence between $\mathrm{coCart}(X)$ and algebras over $\mathrm{hc}\tau_d(X)$. Restricting to $\infty$-groupoid valued algebras gives left fibrations over $X$.

source.note: Heuts defines coCartesian fibrations of dendroidal sets and proves that coCart(X) is equivalent to algebras in ∞-categories over the simplicial operad of X; the steps outline that route.

concepts.c:cocartesian-fibration-of-infinity-1-op: These fibrations are the targets of the equivalence.
concepts.c:grothendieck-construction: The categorical construction that is generalized to operads.
concepts.c:infinity-1-operad: The base operad over which algebras and fibrations live.
concepts.c:infinity-algebra-over-an-infinity-1-op: Algebras are the objects that the construction turns into fibrations.

statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $P$ a $\Sigma$-cofibrant [operad](c:operad) in simplicial $R$-modules. Normalization is lax symmetric monoidal, so it gives an equivalence between the homotopy theories of $P$-[algebras](c:algebra-over-an-operad) in simplicial $R$-modules and of $NP$-algebras in connective [chain complexes](c:chain-complex).

hypotheses.text: $R$ is a commutative ring.
$P$ is a $\Sigma$-cofibrant [operad](c:operad) in simplicial $R$-modules.

conclusion: The normalization functor induces an equivalence between the homotopy theories of $P$-[algebras](c:algebra-over-an-operad) and of $NP$-algebras in connective [chain complexes](c:chain-complex).

proofs.name: Weak monoidal Quillen equivalence
proofs.slogan: Normalization is a lax monoidal equivalence whose shuffle map is a quasi-isomorphism, so it descends to a Quillen equivalence of algebras over a $\Sigma$-cofibrant operad.
proofs.scope: Outline of the method of Schwede and Shipley, as extended to all $\Sigma$-cofibrant operads in the cited work. The model-categorical details rest on that work.

roles.why: The Dold-Kan equivalence between simplicial $R$-modules and connective complexes is stated over $R$.
$\Sigma$-cofibrancy makes free algebras homotopy invariant and lets the model structures transfer.

steps.slogan: Show that normalization is a lax symmetric monoidal equivalence.
steps.detail: By the Dold-Kan correspondence, normalization $N$ is an equivalence from simplicial $R$-modules to connective [chain complexes](c:chain-complex). The shuffle map $NA\otimes NB\to N(A\otimes B)$ makes $N$ lax symmetric monoidal. So $N$ sends the operad $P$ to an operad $NP$ and sends $P$-algebras to $NP$-algebras.

steps.slogan: Show that the shuffle map is a quasi-isomorphism.
steps.detail: The Eilenberg-Zilber theorem says that the shuffle map is a quasi-isomorphism, with the Alexander-Whitney map as homotopy inverse. So $N$ is a weak monoidal Quillen equivalence in the sense of Schwede and Shipley.

steps.slogan: Compare the free algebras on cofibrant objects.
steps.detail: For a $\Sigma$-cofibrant operad, the free algebra $\bigoplus_n P(n)\otimes_{\Sigma_n}A^{\otimes n}$ computes the derived free algebra. The shuffle maps give a comparison map between the two free algebras that is a weak equivalence in each arity.

steps.slogan: Transfer the model structures from the underlying objects to the algebras.
steps.detail: Because $P$ is $\Sigma$-cofibrant, the forgetful functors create model structures on both algebra categories. Weak equivalences and fibrations of algebras are then detected on the underlying objects.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the induced adjunction on algebras is an equivalence of homotopy theories.
steps.detail: The derived unit and counit are weak equivalences on cofibrant algebras, since they are detected on underlying objects and on free generators by the previous steps. So the adjunction is a [Quillen equivalence](c:quillen-equivalence) and induces the stated equivalence of homotopy theories.

source.ref: H. Truong, Operadic Dold-Kan correspondence and mapping spaces between enriched operads, arXiv:2312.07906 (2023); method of S. Schwede and B. Shipley, Equivalences of monoidal model categories, Algebraic & Geometric Topology 3 (2003), 287-334
source.note: Truong proves that the Dold-Kan correspondence for operadic algebras holds for every Sigma-cofibrant operad; the steps follow the weak monoidal Quillen equivalence method of Schwede and Shipley.

concepts.c:algebra-over-an-operad: Algebras are the objects compared across the two homotopy theories.
concepts.c:chain-complex: Connective chain complexes are the target of normalization.
concepts.c:operad: The operad $P$ and its normalization $NP$ carry the algebra structures.
concepts.c:quillen-equivalence: A Quillen equivalence is how the two homotopy theories are identified.

statement: Let a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) $\mathcal M$ act on a category $\mathcal C$ (an [actegory](c:actegory)). The morphisms $X\to Y$ of $\mathrm{Para}_{\mathcal M}(\mathcal C)$ are pairs $(P,f)$ with $f\colon P\bullet X\to Y$, up to isomorphism of $P$; composites are $(Q\otimes P,\ g\circ(Q\bullet f)\circ a)$ and identities are $(I,u_X)$. This is a [category](c:category).

hypotheses.text: $(\mathcal M,\otimes,I)$ is a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) with associator $\alpha$ and unitors $\lambda,\rho$.

The action $\bullet\colon\mathcal M\times\mathcal C\to\mathcal C$ has [natural isomorphisms](c:natural-isomorphism) $a_{Q,P,X}\colon(Q\otimes P)\bullet X\to Q\bullet(P\bullet X)$ and $u_X\colon I\bullet X\to X$ that satisfy the pentagon and triangle axioms.

conclusion: Composition in $\mathrm{Para}_{\mathcal M}(\mathcal C)$ is well defined on classes of pairs, associative and unital.

proofs.name: Coherence check
proofs.slogan: Check that composition respects reparametrization, then reduce the unit and associativity laws to the triangle and pentagon axioms of the action.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for the quotient by isomorphisms of the parameter. Without the quotient the same checks give a bicategory whose 2-cells are the reparametrizations.

roles.why: The tensor product and unit supply the parameters of composites and identities, and $\alpha,\lambda,\rho$ give the reparametrizations.
Naturality of $a$ and $u$ and the pentagon and triangle axioms make the laws hold.

steps.slogan: Fix the morphisms, identities and composites.
steps.detail: A morphism is a class of pairs $(P,f)$ under isomorphisms $r\colon P\to P'$ with $f'\circ(r\bullet X)=f$. Take $(I,u_X)$ as identity. For $f\colon P\bullet X\to Y$ and $g\colon Q\bullet Y\to Z$ take $(Q,g)\circ(P,f)=(Q\otimes P,\ g\circ(Q\bullet f)\circ a_{Q,P,X})$.

steps.slogan: Show that composition respects reparametrization.
steps.detail: Let $r\colon P\to P'$ and $r'\colon Q\to Q'$ reparametrize $f$ and $g$. Then $r'\otimes r$ reparametrizes the first composite into the second. The check uses naturality of $a$, bifunctoriality of $\bullet$ and the equations $f'\circ(r\bullet X)=f$, $g'\circ(r'\bullet Y)=g$.

steps.slogan: Prove the unit laws from naturality of $u$ and the triangle axiom.
steps.detail: Naturality of $u$ gives $u_Y\circ(I\bullet f)=f\circ u_{P\bullet X}$, and the triangle axiom gives $u_{P\bullet X}\circ a_{I,P,X}=\lambda_P\bullet X$. So $(I,u_Y)\circ(P,f)$ is $(P,f)$ reparametrized by $\lambda_P$. The right unit law is the same with $\rho_Q$.

steps.slogan: Prove associativity from naturality of $a$ and the pentagon axiom.
steps.detail: Both bracketings have maps from $(R\otimes Q)\otimes P$ and $R\otimes(Q\otimes P)$. The pentagon axiom gives $(R\bullet a_{Q,P,X})\circ a_{R,Q\otimes P,X}\circ(\alpha\bullet X)=a_{R,Q,P\bullet X}\circ a_{R\otimes Q,P,X}$. Naturality of $a_{R,Q,-}$ then identifies the two maps up to $\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the classes of pairs form a category.
steps.detail: The previous steps show that composition is a well-defined associative operation on classes, with the stated identities. So $\mathrm{Para}_{\mathcal M}(\mathcal C)$ is a [category](c:category).

source.note: Direct coherence check; the construction is that of B. Fong, D. Spivak and R. Tuyéras, Backprop as functor: a compositional perspective on supervised learning, LICS 2019.

concepts.c:actegory: The action and its coherence isomorphisms are what the laws use.
concepts.c:category: The result is that the classes of pairs form a category.
concepts.c:monoidal-category: Its tensor product and unit build parameters of composites and identities.
concepts.c:natural-isomorphism: Naturality of $a$ and $u$ drives every identity check.

hypotheses.text: The payoff $k\colon[0,1]^2\to\mathbb R$ is bounded and continuous off finitely many curves $x=\varphi_i(y)$, $y=\psi_j(x)$ with $\varphi_i,\psi_j$ continuous.
Player I uses only [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-measure) strategies $\mu\in A$, and player II uses any [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\nu\in M$.

conclusion: The [game on the unit square](c:game-on-the-unit-square) with payoff $k(\mu,\nu)=\iint k\,d\mu\,d\nu$ has a value in these strategy sets.

proofs.name: Minimax over absolutely continuous strategies
proofs.slogan: The easy inequality is weak duality; absolutely continuous strategies do not see the discontinuity curves, and a minimax theorem on the mixed extension gives the other inequality.
proofs.scope: Outline of the published proof. Steps 1 to 3 are elementary reductions; the semicontinuity argument inside step 4 rests on the cited paper.

roles.why: Boundedness and continuity off the curves control the sections of $k$ and make the iterated integrals exist.
Restricting player I to densities removes pure strategies, which is the only way the curves can hurt.

steps.slogan: Bound the sup-inf value by the inf-sup value.
steps.detail:
Write $V_-=\sup_\mu\inf_
u k(\mu,
u)$ and $V_+=\inf_
u\sup_\mu k(\mu,
u)$. For all $\mu,
u$ we have $\inf_{
u'}k(\mu,
u')\le k(\mu,
u)\le\sup_{\mu'}k(\mu',
u)$. Taking $\sup_\mu$ on the left and $\inf_
u$ on the right gives $V_-\le V_+$.

steps.slogan: Show that absolutely continuous strategies do not see the discontinuity curves.
steps.detail: For $\mu\in A$, each curve $x=\varphi_i(y)$ meets a horizontal line in one point, a $\mu$-null set. A curve $y=\psi_j(x)$ can carry $\mu$-mass at height $y_0$ only if $\{x:\psi_j(x)=y_0\}$ has positive Lebesgue measure, which happens for countably many $y_0$. By dominated convergence, $y\mapsto k(\mu,y)$ is continuous off one countable set $C$ that does not depend on $\mu$.

steps.slogan: Reduce both sides to extremal problems over points.
steps.detail:
By Fubini, $k(\mu,
u)=\int\! ig(\int k\,d\mu ig)d
u$, so the best reply of player II to $\mu$ is a point: $\inf_
u k(\mu,
u)=\inf_y k(\mu,y)$. The best reply of player I to $
u$ is an essential supremum, because densities can concentrate on any set of positive [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure): $\sup_{\mu\in A}k(\mu,
u)=\operatorname{ess\,sup}_x\int k(x,y)\,d
u(y)$.

steps.slogan: Apply a minimax theorem to the bilinear payoff on the two convex strategy sets.
steps.detail: The payoff is bilinear on the convex sets $A$ and $M$. The cited paper applies a minimax theorem of Ky Fan-Sion type to it, using the regularity of step 2 away from the countable set $C$ and the point and essential-supremum replies of step 3. The treatment of the exceptional heights in $C$ is in the cited work. This gives $V_+\le V_-$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two inequalities to obtain the value of the game.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives $V_-\le V_+$ and step 4 gives $V_+\le V_-$. So $V_-=V_+$, and the [game on the unit square](c:game-on-the-unit-square) has this common number as its value.

source.ref: T. Parthasarathy, On games over the unit square, SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics 19 (1970), 473-476
source.note: Parthasarathy proves that the game has a value when player I is restricted to absolutely continuous strategies; steps 1 to 3 are the elementary reductions and step 4 is the minimax argument of the paper.

concepts.c:absolutely-continuous-measure: Absolutely continuous strategies cannot charge the discontinuity curves.
concepts.c:game-on-the-unit-square: The statement is a value theorem for such a game.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Densities concentrate on sets of positive Lebesgue measure, giving the essential supremum.
concepts.c:probability-measure: Mixed strategies are probability measures on the interval.

statement: Let $P$ be an interior point of a [disk](c:ball) of radius $R$. Four lines through $P$ with consecutive angles $\pi/4$ cut the disk into eight [sectors](c:sector-area). The four alternate sectors have total area $\pi R^2/2$, the same as the other four.

hypotheses.text: The disk has center $O$ and radius $R$, and $P$ is an interior point of it.
Four lines through $P$ make consecutive angles $\pi/4$ and cut the disk into eight sectors.

conclusion: The areas of the four alternate sectors add up to $\pi R^2/2$, equal to the total of the other four.

proofs.name: Polar integral
proofs.slogan: Write sector areas as polar integrals about $P$, pair opposite sectors by the chord relations, and cancel the oscillating terms.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, including $P=O$, where all distances equal $R$ and the cosine terms vanish.

roles.why: The circle and the interior point $P$ give the distances $r(t)$ and the chord relations.
The equal angles $\pi/4$ make opposite sectors start at angles that differ by $\pi/2$ in pairs.

steps.slogan: Write each sector area as a polar integral about $P$.
steps.detail: Let $r(t)$ be the distance from $P$ to the [circle](c:circle) along the ray at angle $t$. The disk is convex, so each ray from $P$ meets the circle once. A sector between angles $t_1$ and $t_2$ has area $\tfrac12\int_{t_1}^{t_2}r(t)^2\,dt$.

steps.slogan: Relate the distances on two opposite rays.
steps.detail: Let $d=|OP|$ and let $\varphi$ be the direction of $OP$. The chord through $P$ at angle $t$ lies at distance $d|\sin(t-\varphi)|$ from $O$, so $r(t)+r(t+\pi)=2\sqrt{R^2-d^2\sin^2(t-\varphi)}$. The intersecting chords theorem gives $r(t)\,r(t+\pi)=R^2-d^2$.

steps.slogan: Compute the sum of the squares of two opposite distances.
steps.detail: Write $r=r(t)$ and $r'=r(t+\pi)$. Then $r^2+r'^2=(r+r')^2-2rr'$, and the two chord relations turn this into $4R^2-4d^2\sin^2(t-\varphi)-2R^2+2d^2=2R^2+2d^2\cos2(t-\varphi)$.

steps.slogan: Add the areas of two opposite sectors.
steps.detail: The sectors on $[\theta,\theta+\pi/4]$ and $[\theta+\pi,\theta+5\pi/4]$ are opposite. By the last step their total [area](c:sector-area) is $\tfrac12\int_\theta^{\theta+\pi/4}(r^2+r'^2)\,dt=\tfrac{\pi R^2}{4}+d^2\int_\theta^{\theta+\pi/4}\cos2(t-\varphi)\,dt$.

steps.slogan: Cancel the oscillating terms of two opposite pairs.
steps.detail: The four alternate sectors form two opposite pairs that start at $\theta$ and $\theta+\pi/2$. Since $\cos2(t+\pi/2-\varphi)=-\cos2(t-\varphi)$, the two cosine integrals cancel, and the total is $2\cdot\pi R^2/4=\pi R^2/2$. The other four sectors start at $\theta+\pi/4$ and give the same total.

source.note: Polar-integral computation with the intersecting chords theorem; see L. Carter and S. Wagon, Proof without words: fair allocation of a pizza, Mathematics Magazine 67 (1994), 267-268, for a dissection proof.

concepts.c:ball: The disk is the region cut into sectors from the point $P$.
concepts.c:circle: The boundary circle defines the distance $r(t)$ from $P$.
concepts.c:sector-area: Sector areas are the quantities that the theorem compares.

statement: Let $F\to E\to B$ be a [fibration](c:fibration) sequence of connected [nilpotent spaces](c:nilpotent-space). Then the [rationalizations](c:rationalization) form a fibration sequence $F_{\mathbb Q}\to E_{\mathbb Q}\to B_{\mathbb Q}$.

hypotheses.text: $F\to E\to B$ is a [fibration](c:fibration) sequence of connected spaces.
The spaces $F$, $E$ and $B$ are [nilpotent spaces](c:nilpotent-space).

conclusion: The rationalized maps $F_{\mathbb Q}\to E_{\mathbb Q}\to B_{\mathbb Q}$ form a fibration sequence, so $F_{\mathbb Q}$ is the homotopy fiber of $E_{\mathbb Q}\to B_{\mathbb Q}$.

proofs.name: Homotopy groups of the rationalized fiber
proofs.slogan: Compare $F$ with the fiber of the rationalized map, show by exactness and the five lemma that it has the rationalized homotopy groups, and identify it as $F_{\mathbb Q}$.
proofs.scope: The nilpotent case of the fibre lemma. Bousfield and Kan prove a more general version, where $\pi_1(B)$ acts nilpotently on $H_*(F;\mathbb Q)$; it is not proved here.

roles.why: The fibration gives the long exact sequence of [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) and the comparison of fibers.
Nilpotence makes rationalization of groups exact and lets the fiber be identified as a rationalization.

steps.slogan: Compare $F$ with the fiber $F'$ of the rationalized map.
steps.detail: Replace $E_{\mathbb Q}\to B_{\mathbb Q}$ by a fibration and let $F'$ be its fiber. The localization maps $E\to E_{\mathbb Q}$ and $B\to B_{\mathbb Q}$ commute with the projections, so they induce a map $F\to F'$.

steps.slogan: Show that rationalization keeps the long exact sequence exact.
steps.detail: For $n\ge2$ the sequence of groups $\pi_n(-)\otimes\mathbb Q$ is exact because $\mathbb Q$ is flat. In low degrees localization of nilpotent groups is exact (Hilton, Mislin, Roitberg). So $\pi_2(B)_{\mathbb Q}\to\pi_1(F)_{\mathbb Q}\to\pi_1(E)_{\mathbb Q}\to\pi_1(B)_{\mathbb Q}\to1$ is exact.

steps.slogan: Use the five lemma to compute the homotopy groups of $F'$.
steps.detail: The long exact sequence of $F'\to E_{\mathbb Q}\to B_{\mathbb Q}$ and the rationalized sequence of $F$ agree on the terms of $E$ and $B$. The five lemma, in its form for groups, shows that $\pi_n(F)_{\mathbb Q}\to\pi_n(F')$ is an isomorphism for $n\ge1$. The fiber $F'$ is connected because $\pi_1(E_{\mathbb Q})\to\pi_1(B_{\mathbb Q})$ is onto.

steps.slogan: Identify $F'$ as the rationalization of $F$.
steps.detail: The fiber of a map of connected nilpotent spaces is nilpotent, and by the last step its [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) are rational. A map from the nilpotent space $F$ to a nilpotent rational space that rationalizes every homotopy group is a [rationalization](c:rationalization). So $F'\simeq F_{\mathbb Q}$, and $F_{\mathbb Q}\to E_{\mathbb Q}\to B_{\mathbb Q}$ is a fibration sequence.

source.note: Homotopy-group argument for nilpotent spaces; see P. Hilton, G. Mislin and J. Roitberg, Localization of nilpotent groups and spaces (North-Holland, 1975), Chapter II, and A. K. Bousfield and D. M. Kan, Homotopy limits, completions and localizations, Lecture Notes in Math. 304 (1972), Chapter II.

concepts.c:fibration: The given sequence supplies the long exact sequence and the fibers.
concepts.c:homotopy-group: The proof compares the homotopy groups of $F$ and $F'$.
concepts.c:nilpotent-space: Nilpotence makes localization exact and gives a rationalization.
concepts.c:rationalization: The conclusion identifies the fiber as the rationalization of $F$.

statement: Let $A$ and $B$ be associative algebras over a field $F$, each satisfying a nonzero [polynomial identity](c:polynomial-identity). Then the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) $A\otimes_F B$ also satisfies a nonzero polynomial identity.

hypotheses.text: $A$ and $B$ are associative algebras over a field $F$.
The algebra $A$ satisfies a nonzero [polynomial identity](c:polynomial-identity).
The algebra $B$ satisfies a nonzero polynomial identity.

conclusion: The algebra $A\otimes_F B$ is a PI algebra: it satisfies a nonzero multilinear polynomial identity.

proofs.name: Codimension growth
proofs.slogan: The codimensions of a PI algebra grow at most exponentially, those of a tensor product are at most the product, and $n!$ outgrows every exponential.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for associative algebras over a field; a nonzero identity is first linearized to a multilinear identity.

roles.why: The tensor product algebra evaluates multilinear polynomials on pure tensors factor by factor.
A multilinear identity of $A$ of degree $d_A$ bounds the codimensions of $A$ exponentially.
A multilinear identity of $B$ of degree $d_B$ bounds the codimensions of $B$ exponentially.

steps.slogan: Relate polynomial identities to the codimension sequence.
steps.detail: Let $P_n$ be the $n!$-dimensional space of multilinear polynomials in $x_1,\dots,x_n$, let $T(C)$ be the identities of $C$, and let $c_n(C)=\dim P_n/(P_n\cap T(C))$ be the [codimension sequence](c:codimension-sequence). If $c_n(C)<n!$ then $C$ satisfies a nonzero multilinear identity. A nonzero identity linearizes to a nonzero multilinear identity of some degree $d$.

steps.slogan: Bound the codimension of $A\otimes B$ by the product of the codimensions.
steps.detail: Choose monomials $m_\tau$ that form a basis of $P_n$ modulo $T(A)$, and $m_{\tau'}$ modulo $T(B)$. For each monomial $m_\sigma$, $m_\sigma(a_i\otimes b_i)=m_\sigma(a)\otimes m_\sigma(b)$ is a combination of the $c_n(A)c_n(B)$ elements $m_\tau(a)\otimes m_{\tau'}(b)$. By multilinearity this holds on all of $A\otimes B$, so $c_n(A\otimes B)\le c_n(A)c_n(B)$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite monomials until no increasing subsequence of length $d$ remains.
steps.detail: Let $A$ satisfy a multilinear identity of degree $d$, written $x_1\cdots x_d=\sum_{\sigma\ne\mathrm{id}}\alpha_\sigma x_{\sigma(1)}\cdots x_{\sigma(d)}$ after renaming the variables. If the word $x_{\pi(1)}\cdots x_{\pi(n)}$ for a [permutation](c:permutation) $\pi$ has an increasing subsequence of length $d$, cut it into blocks that start at those letters and substitute the blocks into the identity. Every new word is lexicographically larger, so the process ends. Hence $P_n$ is spanned modulo $T(A)$ by words with no such subsequence.

steps.slogan: Count the permutations without an increasing subsequence of length $d$.
steps.detail: Label each position by the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends there. The positions with equal label form a decreasing subsequence, so there are at most $d-1$ of them. Such a permutation is fixed by the position set and the value set of each part, giving at most $(d-1)^{2n}$ permutations, so $c_n(A)\le(d-1)^{2n}$.

steps.slogan: Compare $\big((d_A-1)(d_B-1)\big)^{2n}$ with $n!$ for large $n$.
steps.detail: The steps above give $c_n(A\otimes B)\le\big((d_A-1)(d_B-1)\big)^{2n}$. By Stirling's approximation $n!$ outgrows every exponential, so $c_n(A\otimes B)<n!$ for large $n$. By the first step, $A\otimes B$ satisfies a nonzero multilinear identity.

source.note: Codimension proof of A. Regev, Existence of identities in A⊗B, Israel Journal of Mathematics 11 (1972), 131-152; see also A. Giambruno and M. Zaicev, Polynomial Identities and Asymptotic Methods (AMS, 2005).

concepts.c:codimension-sequence: Its growth measures how far the algebra is from satisfying no identity.
concepts.c:permutation: Multilinear monomials correspond to permutations of the variables.
concepts.c:polynomial-identity: The hypothesis and the conclusion are both statements about polynomial identities.
concepts.c:tensor-product: The algebra $A\otimes_F B$ is the object that must satisfy an identity.

statement: Wedges of [anti de Sitter spacetime](c:anti-de-sitter-spacetime) correspond to double cones of its conformal boundary. The assignment $\mathcal B(O_W)=\mathcal A(W)$ is a one-to-one correspondence between causal AdS-covariant [local nets](c:local-net) on the bulk and causal conformally covariant nets of a [conformal field theory](c:conformal-field-theory) on the boundary. It matches vacua and positive-energy representations.

hypotheses.text: A bulk theory is a causal [local net](c:local-net) of algebras on anti de Sitter spacetime, covariant under the AdS group, with an invariant vacuum.
A boundary theory is a causal net of algebras on the conformal boundary, covariant under the conformal group, with an invariant vacuum.

conclusion: Identifying bulk wedge algebras with boundary double-cone algebras is a one-to-one correspondence of bulk and boundary theories that preserves vacua and positive energy.

proofs.name: Wedge algebras and double cones
proofs.slogan: Match AdS wedges with boundary double cones, define each theory from the other through these algebras, and check that the two assignments are inverse.
proofs.scope: Outline of the published proof of algebraic holography. The technical verifications of isotony, causality and covariance rest on the cited work.

roles.why: The bulk net supplies the wedge algebras $\mathcal A(W)$ that become boundary algebras.
The boundary net supplies the double-cone algebras $\mathcal B(O)$ that become wedge algebras.

steps.slogan: Match the wedges of the bulk with the double cones of the boundary.
steps.detail: Each double cone $O$ of the boundary determines a wedge $W_O$ of [anti de Sitter spacetime](c:anti-de-sitter-spacetime), and every wedge arises so. The bijection $O\mapsto W_O$ commutes with the action of the common symmetry group and respects inclusion and spacelike separation.

steps.slogan: Restrict a bulk net to a boundary net through the wedge algebras.
steps.detail: Given a causal [local net](c:local-net) $\mathcal A$ on the bulk, put $\mathcal B(O)=\mathcal A(W_O)$. Isotony, locality and covariance of $\mathcal B$ follow from those of $\mathcal A$ through the dictionary of step 1. So $\mathcal B$ is a causal conformally covariant net.

steps.slogan: Build a bulk net from a boundary net through the same dictionary.
steps.detail: Given a causal conformal net $\mathcal B$ on the boundary, put $\mathcal A(W_O)=\mathcal B(O)$ for wedges, and extend to other bulk regions by intersecting wedge algebras. Isotony, causality and covariance of $\mathcal A$ follow from step 1 and the properties of $\mathcal B$.

steps.slogan: Check that the two assignments are inverse to each other.
steps.detail: Restriction after extension returns $\mathcal B(O)=\mathcal A(W_O)$ by definition. Extension after restriction returns the wedge algebras of $\mathcal A$, and a bulk net is determined by its wedge algebras. So the correspondence is one-to-one.

steps.slogan: Transport vacua and positive-energy representations through the correspondence.
steps.detail: The symmetry groups act compatibly by step 1 and the algebras are the same, so an invariant vacuum state of one theory is an invariant vacuum state of the other. Positive-energy representations correspond in the same way.

source.ref: K.-H. Rehren, Algebraic holography, Annales Henri Poincaré 1 (2000), 607-623
source.note: Rehren proves a one-to-one correspondence between causal AdS-covariant theories and causal conformally covariant theories on the boundary, by identifying wedge algebras with double-cone algebras.

concepts.c:anti-de-sitter-spacetime: Its wedges are the bulk regions that are matched with boundary regions.
concepts.c:conformal-field-theory: The boundary theory is a conformally covariant net on the boundary.
concepts.c:local-net: The bulk theory is a local net whose wedge algebras are restricted.

statement: In a [triangle](c:triangle) $ABC$, let the [cevians](c:cevian) $AA'$, $BB'$, $CC'$ meet at a point, with $A',B',C'$ on the side lines. The circle $\omega$ through $A',B',C'$ meets the side lines again at $A'',B'',C''$, none a vertex. Then $AA''$, $BB''$, $CC''$ are concurrent, or all parallel.

hypotheses.text: $ABC$ is a [triangle](c:triangle), and $A',B',C'$ lie on the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ and differ from the vertices.
The [cevians](c:cevian) $AA'$, $BB'$, $CC'$ are concurrent.
The circle $\omega$ through $A',B',C'$ meets the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ again at $A'',B'',C''$ (a tangency counts twice), and these differ from the vertices.

conclusion: The lines $AA''$, $BB''$, $CC''$ are concurrent, or all parallel.

proofs.name: Ceva and power of a point
proofs.slogan: Express the ratio product of the new cevians through the power of each vertex with respect to the circle, and compare it with Ceva's condition for the old cevians.
proofs.scope: The whole statement with directed lengths on each side line. The points $A',B',C'$ are not collinear, since concurrent cevians give Ceva product $+1$ and collinear points give Menelaus product $-1$, so the circle exists.

roles.why: The vertices lie on two side lines each, so the power of a vertex is a product along either line.
Concurrency gives Ceva's condition for the cevians $AA'$, $BB'$, $CC'$.
The second intersections give the products to compare, and none is zero.

steps.slogan: Write Ceva's condition for the original cevians with directed lengths.
steps.detail: Ceva's theorem gives $\frac{BA'}{A'C}\cdot\frac{CB'}{B'A}\cdot\frac{AC'}{C'B}=1$. Since $A'C=-CA'$, $B'A=-AB'$ and $C'B=-BC'$, this says $\frac{BA'\cdot CB'\cdot AC'}{CA'\cdot AB'\cdot BC'}=-1$.

steps.slogan: Apply the power of a point at each vertex.
steps.detail: Each vertex lies on two side lines that meet $\omega$ twice. Directed lengths give $BA'\cdot BA''=BC'\cdot BC''$, $CB'\cdot CB''=CA'\cdot CA''$ and $AC'\cdot AC''=AB'\cdot AB''$. No product is zero because the points differ from the vertices.

steps.slogan: Eliminate $A'',B'',C''$ from the ratio product of the new cevians.
steps.detail: Solve the three equations for $BA''$, $CA''$ and $AB''$. In $\frac{BA''}{A''C}\cdot\frac{CB''}{B''A}\cdot\frac{AC''}{C''B}$ all lengths with double primes cancel, and the product equals $-\frac{BC'\cdot CA'\cdot AB'}{BA'\cdot CB'\cdot AC'}$.

steps.slogan: Compare with Ceva's condition and apply the converse of Ceva's theorem.
steps.detail: Step 1 says $X=\frac{BA'\cdot CB'\cdot AC'}{CA'\cdot AB'\cdot BC'}=-1$. The expression of step 3 is $-1/X=1$, so the new ratio product is $1$. By the converse of Ceva's theorem, $AA''$, $BB''$, $CC''$ are concurrent or parallel.

source.note: Computation with Ceva's theorem and the power of a point; the theorem is named after K. G. Reuschle and O. Terquem (1842).

concepts.c:cevian: The theorem compares two triples of cevians.
concepts.c:triangle: The vertices and side lines give the powers and ratios.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a [triangle](c:triangle) of area $S$, and let $D,E,F$ lie inside $BC,CA,AB$ with $CD/BD=x$, $AE/CE=y$, $BF/AF=z$. The triangle bounded by the [cevians](c:cevian) $AD$, $BE$, $CF$ has area $S\,\dfrac{(xyz-1)^2}{(xy+y+1)(yz+z+1)(zx+x+1)}$.

hypotheses.text: $ABC$ is a [triangle](c:triangle) of area $S$.
The points $D,E,F$ lie inside the sides $BC,CA,AB$, and $x=CD/BD$, $y=AE/CE$, $z=BF/AF$ are positive reals.

proofs.name: Barycentric determinant
proofs.slogan: Write the three cevians in barycentric coordinates, find the vertices of the inner triangle, and compute its area as a determinant.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for interior points. The area is $0$ exactly when $xyz=1$, the case of concurrent cevians.

roles.why: The triangle is the reference triangle of the barycentric coordinates, and $S$ scales all areas.
The ratios $x,y,z$ fix the barycentric coordinates of $D,E,F$.

steps.slogan: Place $D$, $E$, $F$ in barycentric coordinates.
steps.detail: From $CD/BD=x$ we get $D=(xB+C)/(1+x)$, so $D=(0:x:1)$. In the same way $AE/CE=y$ gives $E=(1:0:y)$, and $BF/AF=z$ gives $F=(z:1:0)$.

steps.slogan: Intersect the [cevians](c:cevian) pairwise to find the three vertices.
steps.detail: The lines are $AD\colon b=xc$, $BE\colon c=ya$ and $CF\colon a=zb$. Their pairwise intersections are $AD\cap BE=(1:xy:y)$, $BE\cap CF=(z:1:yz)$ and $CF\cap AD=(xz:x:1)$.

steps.slogan: Express the inner area by a determinant of the vertex coordinates.
steps.detail: A triangle with normalized barycentric vertices $r_1,r_2,r_3$ has [area](c:area) $S\,|\det(r_1,r_2,r_3)|$. Normalizing divides the three rows by their sums $xy+y+1$, $yz+z+1$ and $zx+x+1$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the [determinant](c:determinant) of the unnormalized rows.
steps.detail: Expand the determinant of the rows $(1,xy,y)$, $(z,1,yz)$, $(xz,x,1)$ along the first row. It equals $(1-xyz)-xy(z-xyz^2)+y(xz-xz)$, which is $(1-xyz)^2$.

steps.slogan: Divide by the three row sums to obtain the area.
steps.detail: The inner triangle has area $S\,(1-xyz)^2/\big((xy+y+1)(yz+z+1)(zx+x+1)\big)$, which is the stated formula because $(1-xyz)^2=(xyz-1)^2$.

source.note: Barycentric-coordinate computation; the area formula for a triangle in barycentric coordinates is standard.

concepts.c:area: The area ratio is the quantity computed.
concepts.c:cevian: The inner triangle is bounded by three cevians.
concepts.c:determinant: The area ratio equals a determinant of vertex coordinates.
concepts.c:triangle: The reference triangle supplies barycentric coordinates and the area $S$.

statement: Let $H$ and $K$ be real [Hilbert spaces](c:hilbert-space) and $T\colon H\to K$ a [Hilbert-Schmidt operator](c:hilbert-schmidt-operator). Then $T$ is $\gamma$-radonifying: the image under $T$ of the canonical Gaussian cylinder measure $\gamma_H$ extends to a Radon [Gaussian measure](c:gaussian-measure) on $K$.

hypotheses.text: $H$ and $K$ are real [Hilbert spaces](c:hilbert-space).
$T\colon H\to K$ is a [Hilbert-Schmidt operator](c:hilbert-schmidt-operator): $\sum_i\|Te_i\|^2<\infty$ for an orthonormal basis $(e_i)$ of $H$.

conclusion: The cylinder measure $T_*\gamma_H$ extends to a Radon [Gaussian measure](c:gaussian-measure) on $K$.

proofs.name: Gaussian series
proofs.slogan: Build a Gaussian random series $\sum_i\gamma_iTe_i$, show that it converges in $L^2$ by the Hilbert-Schmidt condition, and read off its law and characteristic functional.
proofs.scope: The case of separable $H$. A Hilbert-Schmidt operator vanishes on all but countably many vectors of any orthonormal basis, so the general case reduces to a separable subspace.

roles.why: Completeness of $K$ gives the limit of the series, and an orthonormal basis of $H$ indexes it.
The finite sum $\sum_i\|Te_i\|^2$ makes the partial sums Cauchy in $L^2$.

steps.slogan: Expand $T$ along an orthonormal basis of $H$.
steps.detail: Take an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) $(e_i)_{i\ge1}$ of $H$. The Hilbert-Schmidt condition gives $\sum_i\|Te_i\|^2=\|T\|_{HS}^2<\infty$. The closed span $K_0$ of $T(H)$ is a separable subspace of $K$.

steps.slogan: Show that the Gaussian series $\sum_i\gamma_iTe_i$ is Cauchy in $L^2$.
steps.detail: Let $(\gamma_i)$ be independent standard normal variables and $X_n=\sum_{i\le n}\gamma_iTe_i$. Since $E[\gamma_i\gamma_j]=\delta_{ij}$, $E\|X_n-X_m\|^2=\sum_{m<i\le n}\|Te_i\|^2\to0$. So $(X_n)$ is a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) in $L^2(\Omega;K)$.

steps.slogan: Take the limit and read off a Radon measure.
steps.detail: The space $L^2(\Omega;K)$ is complete, so $X_n\to X$ with values in the separable space $K_0$. The law $\mu$ of $X$ is a Borel probability measure on a Polish space, so it is a Radon measure on $K$ (Ulam's theorem).

steps.slogan: Compute the characteristic functional of the limit.
steps.detail: For $y\in K$, $\langle X,y\rangle=\lim_n\sum_{i\le n}\gamma_i\langle e_i,T^*y\rangle$ is an $L^2$-limit of centered Gaussian variables. So it is centered Gaussian with variance $\sum_i\langle e_i,T^*y\rangle^2=\|T^*y\|^2$ by Parseval. Hence $\hat\mu(y)=e^{-\|T^*y\|^2/2}$, the characteristic functional of $T_*\gamma_H$, and $\mu$ is a [Gaussian measure](c:gaussian-measure) that extends it.

source.note: Standard argument with a Gaussian series; see for example V. I. Bogachev, Gaussian Measures (AMS, 1998).

concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: Cauchy in $L^2$ gives convergence of the partial sums.
concepts.c:gaussian-measure: The extension is a Gaussian measure with the computed characteristic functional.
concepts.c:hilbert-schmidt-operator: The summability of $\|Te_i\|^2$ is the hypothesis that drives convergence.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: Completeness of $K$ and the basis of $H$ are used.
concepts.c:orthonormal-basis: The basis indexes the independent Gaussian coefficients of the series.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a [triangle](c:triangle). The circle $C_1$ touches $AB$ and $AC$. The circles $C_2,\dots,C_6$ lie in the angles at $B,C,A,B,C$ in turn, and each $C_{i+1}$ touches two sides and is the smaller circle [tangent](c:tangent-circles) to $C_i$. If all circles lie in the triangle, then $C_6$ is tangent to $C_1$.

hypotheses.text: $ABC$ is a [triangle](c:triangle) with sides $a,b,c$ and semiperimeter $s$.
The circles $C_1,\dots,C_6$ lie in the triangle and are inscribed in the angles at $A,B,C,A,B,C$ in turn, and each $C_{i+1}$ is the smaller circle that is [tangent](c:tangent-circles) to $C_i$.

conclusion: The circle $C_6$ is tangent to $C_1$, so the chain closes after six circles.

proofs.name: Tangent lengths and reflections
proofs.slogan: Describe each circle by a tangent length, rewrite tangency as a law of cosines with a common circumradius, and see that each step reflects an angle.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The hypothesis that all circles lie in the triangle keeps each angle $\varphi_i$ below the next $\theta$, so every next circle exists.

roles.why: The sides and semiperimeter give the common circumradius $\sqrt s/2$ of the three auxiliary triangles.
The chain of tangent circles in the angles gives the relations that are composed.

steps.slogan: Express tangency along a side through the tangent lengths.
steps.detail: A circle in the angle at $V$ with tangent length $u$ has radius $u\tan\frac V2$. Two circles in the angles at $V,W$ that touch the side $VW$ on the same side satisfy $\mathrm{gap}^2+(r_1-r_2)^2=(r_1+r_2)^2$ when [tangent](c:tangent-circles), so $\mathrm{gap}^2=4r_1r_2$. For the smaller circle this reads $VW-u-v=2\sqrt{uv\tan\frac V2\tan\frac W2}$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the relation with the semiperimeter and an angle $\theta$.
steps.detail: With the radius $r$ of the [incircle](c:incircle), $\tan\frac V2=\frac{r}{s-\text{(opposite side)}}$ and $r^2s=(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)$ by Heron's formula. Hence $\tan\frac V2\tan\frac W2=\frac{s-VW}{s}$. Put $u=p^2$, $v=q^2$, $\cos\theta=\sqrt{(s-VW)/s}$ with $0<\theta<\pi/2$. Then $\sin\theta=\sqrt{VW/s}$ and the relation is $p^2+q^2+2pq\cos\theta=s\sin^2\theta$.

steps.slogan: Parametrize the relation by an angle $\varphi$.
steps.detail: A triangle with sides $p,q$ and included angle $\pi-\theta$ has third side $\sqrt s\sin\theta$ by the law of cosines, and circumradius $\sqrt s/2$ by the law of sines. So $p=\sqrt s\sin\varphi$ and $q=\sqrt s\sin(\theta-\varphi)$ with $0<\varphi<\theta$. For given $p$ this is the only positive $q$, because the quadratic in $q$ has root product $p^2-s\sin^2\theta<0$.

steps.slogan: Follow the chain: each step reflects the angle $\varphi$.
steps.detail: Define $\varphi_i\in(0,\pi/2)$ by $p_i=\sqrt s\sin\varphi_i$ for $C_i$, and let $\theta_c,\theta_a,\theta_b$ belong to the sides $AB,BC,CA$. By the last step $\varphi_{i+1}=\theta-\varphi_i$, where $\theta$ belongs to the side shared by $C_i$ and $C_{i+1}$. Along $AB,BC,CA,AB,BC,CA$ the angle runs $\varphi_1\mapsto\theta_c-\varphi_1\mapsto\theta_a-\theta_c+\varphi_1\mapsto\theta_b-\theta_a+\theta_c-\varphi_1\mapsto\theta_a-\theta_b+\varphi_1\mapsto\theta_b-\varphi_1\mapsto\varphi_1$.

steps.slogan: Read off the tangency of $C_6$ and $C_1$ from the return of the angle.
steps.detail: After six steps the angle is again $\varphi_1$, so the next circle in the angle at $A$ has $p=p_1$. That circle is $C_1$, and it is tangent to $C_6$ along $CA$ by construction. Hence $C_6$ is tangent to $C_1$.

source.note: Elementary proof by tangent lengths; for chains of circles in a triangle see D. Ivanov and S. Tabachnikov, The six circles theorem revisited, American Mathematical Monthly 123 (2016), 689-698.

concepts.c:incircle: Its radius turns half-angle tangents into the semiperimeter.
concepts.c:tangent-circles: Tangency of consecutive circles is the relation that is iterated.
concepts.c:triangle: Its sides, angles and semiperimeter fix all the tangent-length relations.

statement: Let $p$ be an odd [prime](c:prime-number) such that $q=2p+1$ is also prime. If integers $x,y,z$ satisfy $x^p+y^p=z^p$, then $p$ divides $xyz$.

hypotheses.text: $p$ is an odd [prime number](c:prime-number).
$q=2p+1$ is a prime number.
The integers $x,y,z$ satisfy $x^p+y^p=z^p$.

proofs.name: Residues modulo $2p+1$
proofs.slogan: Assume $p\nmid xyz$, split the equation into $p$-th powers, and use that $p$-th powers modulo $q$ are $0$ or $\pm1$ to reach a contradiction.
proofs.scope: The whole statement; the case $xyz=0$ is trivial since $p\mid0$. The proof is the first case of Fermat's equation for $p$ with $2p+1$ prime.

roles.why: Oddness of $p$ absorbs signs in $p$-th powers, and $p\nmid ABC$ keeps the two factors coprime.
Since $q=2p+1$, every $p$-th power is $0$ or $\pm1$ modulo $q$, and $p\not\equiv0,\pm1$.
The equation gives the relation $A^p+B^p+C^p=0$ that is split and reduced.

steps.slogan: Assume $p\nmid xyz$ and reduce to a coprime triple.
steps.detail:
Suppose $p
mid xyz$. Dividing by the [greatest common divisor](c:greatest-common-divisor) keeps $p
mid xyz$ and makes $x,y,z$ pairwise coprime. Put $A=x$, $B=y$, $C=-z$. Then $A^p+B^p+C^p=0$, the numbers are pairwise coprime, and $p
mid ABC$.

steps.slogan: Show that $A+B$ and its cofactor are both $p$-th powers.
steps.detail: Write $(A+B)\Phi_{AB}=-C^p$ with $\Phi_{AB}=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}A^{p-1-i}(-B)^i\equiv pA^{p-1}\pmod{A+B}$. A common prime divisor is $p$ or divides $A$. The first gives $p\mid C$ by Fermat's little theorem, the second contradicts $\gcd(A,B)=1$. So the factors are coprime, and both are $p$-th powers, $A+B=u^p$ and $\Phi_{AB}=u'^p$. The same holds for the pairs $(B,C)$ and $(C,A)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $q$ divides one of $A$, $B$, $C$.
steps.detail: If $q\nmid t$ then $(t^p)^2=t^{q-1}\equiv1\pmod q$ by Fermat, so $t^p\equiv\pm1$. If $q\nmid ABC$, the sum $A^p+B^p+C^p$ is a sum of three terms $\pm1$, hence $\pm1$ or $\pm3$, never $0$ [modulo](c:modular-arithmetic) $q\ge7$. So $q$ divides one of them, say $q\mid A$.

steps.slogan: Show that $B\equiv-C\equiv\pm1$ modulo $q$.
steps.detail: From $q\mid A$, $A+B=u^p$ and $A+C=w^p$ we get $B\equiv u^p$ and $C\equiv w^p\pmod q$. Neither is $0$ since the numbers are coprime, so $B,C\equiv\pm1$ and $B^p\equiv B$, $C^p\equiv C$. Then $B^p+C^p\equiv-A^p\equiv0$ gives $C\equiv-B$.

steps.slogan: Reach a contradiction from $\Phi_{BC}\equiv p\pmod q$.
steps.detail: As $C\equiv-B$, every term $B^{p-1-i}(-C)^i\equiv B^{p-1}\equiv1$, so $\Phi_{BC}\equiv p\pmod q$. But $\Phi_{BC}=v'^p\equiv0$ or $\pm1\pmod q$. Since $1<p<p+1<q$, the number $p$ is none of $0,\pm1$ modulo $q$, a contradiction. So $p\mid xyz$.

source.note: Classical proof of Sophie Germain's theorem for the auxiliary prime $2p+1$; see H. M. Edwards, Fermat's Last Theorem: A Genetic Introduction to Algebraic Number Theory (Springer, 1977).

concepts.c:greatest-common-divisor: Dividing by the common divisor gives a pairwise coprime triple.
concepts.c:modular-arithmetic: Residues modulo $q$ carry the whole contradiction.
concepts.c:prime-number: The exponent $p$ and the auxiliary modulus $q$ are primes.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite group. The functor $F\colon\mathrm{Sp}_G\to\mathrm{Fun}^{\times}(\mathrm{Span}(\mathbb F_G),\mathrm{Sp})$ sends a [$G$-spectrum](c:g-spectrum) $X$ to $G/K\mapsto\mathrm{Map}(\Sigma^\infty_{G,+}[G/K],X)$, with transfers from Wirthmüller self-duality. It is an equivalence onto spectral [Mackey functors](c:mackey-functor).

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a finite group.

conclusion: The functor $F$ is an equivalence of $\infty$-categories from $G$-spectra to product-preserving functors from spans of finite $G$-sets to spectra.

proofs.name: Orbit generators and the spectral Burnside category
proofs.slogan: Generate $G$-spectra by orbit suspension spectra, identify their mapping spectra with spans through Wirthmüller duality, and compare presheaves with product-preserving functors.
proofs.scope: Outline of the published proof. The equivariant infinite loop space theory and the model-categorical comparisons rest on the cited work.

roles.why: Finiteness of $G$ gives finitely many orbit types, compact orbit spectra and the Wirthmüller isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Generate the $G$-spectra by the suspension spectra of orbits.
steps.detail: The spectra $\Sigma^\infty_{G,+}[G/H]$ for subgroups $H\le G$ form a set of compact generators of $\mathrm{Sp}_G$. So $\mathrm{Sp}_G$ is equivalent to spectral presheaves on the full spectral subcategory of these orbits.

steps.slogan: Use Wirthmüller duality to obtain transfers between orbits.
steps.detail: The Wirthmüller isomorphism makes $\Sigma^\infty_{G,+}[G/H]$ self-dual over the sphere $G$-spectrum. A map $[G/K]\to[G/H]$ then yields a transfer $\Sigma^\infty_{G,+}[G/H]\to\Sigma^\infty_{G,+}[G/K]$, which enlarges the orbit category to the [Burnside category](c:burnside-category) of spans.

steps.slogan: Identify the mapping spectra between orbits with spans.
steps.detail: By equivariant infinite loop space theory, the mapping spectrum between two orbits is the group completion of the category of spans of finite $G$-sets between them. Composition of spans matches composition in $\mathrm{Sp}_G$.

steps.slogan: Match presheaves on orbits with product-preserving functors on spans.
steps.detail: Spectral presheaves on the spectral Burnside category correspond to product-preserving functors from $\mathrm{Span}(\mathbb F_G)$ to spectra, since group completion makes the spans additive. Under these identifications $F$ is the equivalence of step 1, so it is an equivalence onto spectral [Mackey functors](c:mackey-functor).

source.ref: B. Guillou and J. P. May, Models of G-spectra as presheaves of spectra, Algebraic & Geometric Topology 24 (2024), 1225-1275
source.note: Guillou and May give Quillen equivalent models of G-spectra as spectrally enriched functors on spans of finite G-sets; the steps outline that comparison.

concepts.c:burnside-category: Spans of finite $G$-sets with transfers form the domain category.
concepts.c:g-spectrum: $G$-spectra are the objects that are generated by orbits.
concepts.c:mackey-functor: Spectral Mackey functors are the target of the equivalence.

statement: Let $1\le k\le n-1$, and let $a=\binom{n-1}{k-1}$, $b=\binom n{k+1}$, $c=\binom{n+1}k$ and $a'=\binom{n-1}k$, $b'=\binom n{k-1}$, $c'=\binom{n+1}{k+1}$ be the six [binomial coefficients](c:binomial-coefficient) around $\binom nk$ in [Pascal's triangle](c:pascal-triangle). Then $abc=a'b'c'$ and $\gcd(a,b,c)=\gcd(a',b',c')$.

hypotheses.text: The integers $n$ and $k$ satisfy $1\le k\le n-1$.

conclusion: The two triples have equal products and equal [greatest common divisors](c:greatest-common-divisor).

proofs.name: Factorials and valuations
proofs.slogan: Write the six entries over one numerator, read off the equal products, and compare the exponent of each prime in the two greatest common divisors by cases.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for $1\le k\le n-1$, where all six entries are positive.

roles.why: The range makes all six entries positive and all factorials in the formulas defined.

steps.slogan: Write the six entries with one common numerator $T$.
steps.detail: Put $i=k$, $j=n-k$ and $T=\frac{(n-1)!}{(i-1)!\,(j-1)!}$. By the factorial formula for [binomial coefficients](c:binomial-coefficient), $a=\frac Tj$, $a'=\frac Ti$, $b=\frac{nT}{i(i+1)}$, $b'=\frac{nT}{j(j+1)}$, $c=\frac{n(n+1)T}{ij(j+1)}$ and $c'=\frac{n(n+1)T}{ij(i+1)}$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the entries of each triple to equate the products.
steps.detail: Multiply the three formulas of the last step. Both $abc$ and $a'b'c'$ equal $\frac{n^2(n+1)T^3}{i^2j^2(i+1)(j+1)}$, so $abc=a'b'c'$.

steps.slogan: Reduce the gcd claim to exponents of a prime $p$.
steps.detail: Put $L=ij(i+1)(j+1)$. Then $a,b,c$ equal $T/L$ times $M_1=i(i+1)(j+1)$, $M_2=nj(j+1)$, $M_3=n(n+1)(i+1)$, and $a',b',c'$ equal $T/L$ times $M_1'=j(i+1)(j+1)$, $M_2'=ni(i+1)$, $M_3'=n(n+1)(j+1)$. So it suffices to show $\min_rv_p(M_r)=\min_rv_p(M_r')$ for every prime $p$.

steps.slogan: Treat the primes that divide at most one of $i(i+1)$ and $j(j+1)$.
steps.detail:
Let $X=v_p(i(i+1))$, $Y=v_p(j(j+1))$, $z=v_p(n)$, $W=v_p(n(n+1))$, $x_1=v_p(i+1)$, $y_1=v_p(j+1)$. The exponent triples are $(X+y_1,\ z+Y,\ W+x_1)$ and $(Y+x_1,\ z+X,\ W+y_1)$. If $p
mid i(i+1)j(j+1)$ they are equal. If $p\mid i$ and $p
mid j(j+1)$ they are $(X,0,0)$ and $(0,X,0)$. If $p\mid i+1$ and $p
mid j(j+1)$ they are $(X,z,z+X)$ and $(X,z+X,z)$. Swapping $i$ and $j$ swaps the triples.

steps.slogan: Treat the primes that divide both $i(i+1)$ and $j(j+1)$.
steps.detail: If $p\mid i$ and $p\mid j$, then $z\ge\min(X,Y)$ with equality for $X\ne Y$, $W=z$, and the triples $(X,z+Y,z)$, $(Y,z+X,z)$ both have minimum $\min(X,Y)$. If $p\mid i$ and $p\mid j+1$, or $p\mid i+1$ and $p\mid j$, then $p\mid n+1$, $W\ge\min(X,Y)$ with equality for $X\ne Y$, and both minima are $\min(X,Y)$. If $p\mid i+1$ and $p\mid j+1$, the triples are $(X+Y,z+Y,z+X)$ and $(X+Y,z+X,z+Y)$, equal as multisets.

steps.slogan: Equate the minima for every prime to equate the greatest common divisors.
steps.detail: For every prime $p$ the two minima agree, and the common factor $T/L$ shifts both by the same amount. So $\gcd(a,b,c)$ and $\gcd(a',b',c')$ have the same exponent of every prime. With $abc=a'b'c'$ this is the theorem.

source.note: Elementary proof by valuations; the theorem was conjectured by H. W. Gould and proved by A. P. Hillman and V. E. Hoggatt, A proof of Gould's Pascal hexagon conjecture, Fibonacci Quarterly 10 (1972), 565-568.

concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: The six entries are binomial coefficients, written with factorials.
concepts.c:greatest-common-divisor: The theorem equates the greatest common divisors of two triples.
concepts.c:pascal-triangle: The six entries form the hexagon around $\binom nk$.
